abstract: |
  This report asks whether local equity volatility has risen, how our flagship SafeCore fund copes with it, and whether stock-pickers have more room to add value since 2020. Local volatility has not trended up since 2015, but it comes in episodes, and 2026 is the most volatile year outside of COVID. It moves closely with global volatility (a GARCH volatility correlation of 0.85), but the 2026 spike tracks emerging markets rather than developed markets. In months of high offshore stress, local volatility runs about a third above normal. SafeCore earns alpha but does nothing to dampen volatility, and its risk is now concentrated in gold miners: Resources hold 40% of the weight but 68% of the risk. Dispersion between stocks has recovered to its highest level since 2022, but in stress periods higher dispersion comes with higher correlation. We recommend keeping SafeCore's stock-selection edge while adding a deliberate risk ballast.
---

# Data (each question folder holds its own copy in data/)

Local_Cncy_Vol_Index <- read_rds("data/LCL_Currency_Vol_Index.rds") %>%
  mutate(TRI = ifelse(TRI < 1, TRI * 100, TRI))           # 2021-2026 prints divided by 100
Commods <- read_rds("data/Commodities.rds")
MSCI <- read_rds("data/MSCI_Indexes.rds")
SafeCore <- read_rds("data/SafeCore.rds")

Active_Managers <- read_rds("data/Active_Managers.rds")

  select(date, Tickers, Return = Returns) %>%
  mutate(Return = ifelse(abs(Return) > 0.5, NA, Return))  # data errors

  mutate(Sector = ifelse(is.na(Sector) & Tickers %in% c("PAN", "VAL"), "Resources", Sector)) %>%
  group_by(date) %>% mutate(Weight = Weight / sum(Weight)) %>% ungroup()

# Helpers used throughout
Winsor <- function(x) { q <- quantile(x, c(0.01, 0.99), na.rm = TRUE); pmin(pmax(x, q[1]), q[2]) }
Top_Q <- function(df) df %>% filter(Level > quantile(Level, 0.8)) %>% pull(YearMonth)
Bot_Q <- function(df) df %>% filter(Level < quantile(Level, 0.2)) %>% pull(YearMonth)

Print_Table <- function(df, Caption, Digits = 2, Size = "\\footnotesize") {

               floating = TRUE, table.placement = "H", comment = FALSE,
               include.rownames = FALSE, caption.placement = "top", size = Size)
}

```{r functions, include=FALSE}
# All functions used in this write-up (the same functions as in the code/ folder),
# defined here so the document knits on its own.

# Annualised realised volatility per calendar year, one column per series
# df: tidy frame with columns date, Name, Return (daily simple returns)
Vol_Table <- function(df, Scale = 252) {

  df %>%
    mutate(Year = format(date, "%Y")) %>%
    group_by(Year, Name) %>%
    summarise(Vol = sd(Return, na.rm = TRUE) * sqrt(Scale), .groups = "drop") %>%
    spread(Name, Vol)

}

# Rolling annualised volatility plot
# df: tidy frame with columns date, Name, Return (daily simple returns)
Roll_Vol_Plot <- function(df, Width = 63, Scale = 252, Title = "", Subtitle = "") {

  df_plot <-
    df %>%
    group_by(Name) %>%
    arrange(date) %>%
    mutate(RollVol = RcppRoll::roll_sd(Return, n = Width, fill = NA, align = "right") * sqrt(Scale)) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    filter(!is.na(RollVol))

  g <-
    df_plot %>%
    ggplot() +
    geom_line(aes(date, RollVol, color = Name), alpha = 0.8, linewidth = 0.8) +
    labs(title = Title, subtitle = Subtitle, x = "", y = "Annualised volatility") +
    fmxdat::theme_fmx(title.size = fmxdat::ggpts(30), subtitle.size = fmxdat::ggpts(25),
                      legend.size = fmxdat::ggpts(25), axis.size = fmxdat::ggpts(25))

  fmxdat::finplot(g, y.pct = TRUE, y.pct_acc = 1, x.date.type = "%Y", x.date.dist = "1 year")

}

# Fit an AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) to one return series and return the fit
# Return: xts of demeaned daily log returns (one column)
GARCH_Fit <- function(Return, Model = "gjrGARCH", Dist = "sstd") {

  spec <- rugarch::ugarchspec(
    variance.model = list(model = Model, garchOrder = c(1, 1)),
    mean.model = list(armaOrder = c(1, 0), include.mean = TRUE),
    distribution.model = Dist)

  rugarch::ugarchfit(spec = spec, data = Return, solver = "hybrid")

}

# Compare the four GARCH variants used in Prac 6 on information criteria
GARCH_Compare <- function(Return, Dist = "sstd") {

  Models <- c("sGARCH", "gjrGARCH", "eGARCH", "apARCH")
  model.list <- list()
  for (p in seq_along(Models)) {
    model.list[[p]] <- GARCH_Fit(Return, Model = Models[p], Dist = Dist)
  }
  fit.mat <- sapply(model.list, rugarch::infocriteria)
  colnames(fit.mat) <- Models
  rownames(fit.mat) <- rownames(rugarch::infocriteria(model.list[[1]]))
  fit.mat

}

# Extract annualised conditional volatility from a fit as a tidy frame
GARCH_Sigma <- function(Fit, Name, Scale = 252) {

  rugarch::sigma(Fit) %>%
    tbl2xts::xts_tbl() %>%
    setNames(c("date", "Sigma")) %>%
    mutate(date = as.Date(date), Sigma = Sigma * sqrt(Scale), Name = Name)

}

# Stratification (Prac 2 Bonus): volatility of each series during selected months
# relative to its full-period volatility.
# Idxs: tidy frame with date, YearMonth, Name, Return (winsorised daily returns)
# YMs: vector of YearMonths in the stressed regime; Alias: label for the regime
Perf_comparisons <- function(Idxs, YMs, Alias, Scale = 252) {

  Unconditional_SD <-
    Idxs %>%
    group_by(Name) %>%
    summarise(Full_SD = sd(Return, na.rm = TRUE) * sqrt(Scale), .groups = "drop")

  Idxs %>%
    filter(YearMonth %in% YMs) %>%
    group_by(Name) %>%
    summarise(SD = sd(Return, na.rm = TRUE) * sqrt(Scale), .groups = "drop") %>%
    left_join(Unconditional_SD, by = "Name") %>%
    mutate(Ratio = SD / Full_SD, Period = Alias)

}

# Daily index returns rebuilt from constituent weights and returns
# (weights rescaled to sum to 1 each day)
Index_From_Constituents <- function(Constituents, Indexes) {

  Constituents %>%
    filter(Index %in% Indexes, !is.na(Return)) %>%
    group_by(Index, date) %>%
    mutate(weight = weight / sum(weight, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
    summarise(Return = sum(weight * Return, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
    rename(Name = Index)

}

# Component contribution to portfolio SD (Prac 2) at one rebalance date
# Wts: tidy weights (date, Tickers, Sector, Weight); Rets: tidy daily returns (date, Tickers, Return)
Risk_Contribution <- function(RebDate, Wts, Rets, LookBack = 252) {

  w <- Wts %>% filter(date == RebDate) %>% arrange(Tickers)

  R <-
    Rets %>%
    filter(Tickers %in% w$Tickers, date <= RebDate) %>%
    group_by(Tickers) %>% filter(row_number() > n() - LookBack) %>% ungroup() %>%
    tbl_xts(cols_to_xts = Return, spread_by = Tickers)

  R[is.na(R)] <- 0
  w <- w %>% filter(Tickers %in% colnames(R))
  R <- R[, w$Tickers]

  Contrib <- StdDev(R, weights = w$Weight / sum(w$Weight), portfolio_method = "component")

  tibble(date = RebDate, Tickers = w$Tickers, Sector = w$Sector,
         Weight = w$Weight / sum(w$Weight),
         Risk_Share = as.numeric(Contrib$pct_contrib_StdDev),
         Port_SD = as.numeric(Contrib$StdDev) * sqrt(252))

}

# Own Momentum and Low-Volatility scores from daily price behaviour
# Momentum: 6-month return skipping the most recent month (t-126 to t-21 trading days)
# Low-Vol : minus the 6-month (126-day) annualised realised volatility (higher = calmer stock)
# Both standardised cross-sectionally each month and capped at +-3
Own_Factor_Scores <- function(Rets, MinObs = 126) {

  Raw <-
    Rets %>%
    arrange(Tickers, date) %>%
    group_by(Tickers) %>%
    filter(n() > MinObs) %>%
    mutate(Mom_Raw = lag(RcppRoll::roll_prod(1 + Return, n = 105, fill = NA, align = "right"), 21) - 1,
           Vol_Raw = RcppRoll::roll_sd(Return, n = 126, fill = NA, align = "right") * sqrt(252)) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    mutate(YM = format(date, "%Y%m")) %>%
    group_by(YM) %>% filter(date == max(date)) %>% ungroup()     # last trading day of each month

  Zscore <- function(x) { z <- (x - mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)) / sd(x, na.rm = TRUE); pmin(pmax(z, -3), 3) }

  Raw %>%
    filter(!is.na(Mom_Raw), !is.na(Vol_Raw)) %>%
    group_by(YM) %>%
    mutate(Own_Momentum = Zscore(Mom_Raw), Own_LowVol = Zscore(-Vol_Raw)) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    select(YM, Tickers, Own_Momentum, Own_LowVol)

}

# Daily cross-sectional volatility (dispersion) of index constituents
# Weighted:   sqrt( sum w_i (R_i - Rbar_w)^2 ),  Rbar_w = sum w_i R_i
# Unweighted: plain cross-sectional standard deviation
CSV_Calc <- function(Constituents) {

  Constituents %>%
    filter(!is.na(Return)) %>%
    group_by(date) %>%
    mutate(w = weight / sum(weight)) %>%
    summarise(Weighted = sqrt(sum(w * (Return - sum(w * Return))^2)),
              Unweighted = sd(Return), .groups = "drop")

}

# Average pairwise correlation of the N largest constituents over a trailing window
Avg_Pairwise_Cor <- function(RebDate, Constituents, N = 40, LookBack = 63) {

  Top <-
    Constituents %>% filter(date == RebDate) %>%
    arrange(desc(weight)) %>% head(N) %>% pull(Tickers)

  R <-
    Constituents %>%
    filter(Tickers %in% Top, date <= RebDate, date > RebDate - 2 * LookBack) %>%
    select(date, Tickers, Return) %>%
    spread(Tickers, Return) %>%
    tail(LookBack) %>%
    select(-date)

  C <- cor(R, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
  tibble(date = RebDate, Avg_Cor = mean(C[upper.tri(C)], na.rm = TRUE))

}

# Stratification of a monthly alpha-opportunity measure by macro regime:
# average of each measure in the top and bottom quintile months of a driver, relative to its full-sample mean
# Measures: tidy (YearMonth, Measure, Value); Driver: (YearMonth, Level)
Regime_Means <- function(Measures, Driver, Alias) {

  Hi <- Driver %>% filter(Level > quantile(Level, 0.8, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% pull(YearMonth)
  Lo <- Driver %>% filter(Level < quantile(Level, 0.2, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% pull(YearMonth)

  Measures %>%
    group_by(Measure) %>%
    summarise(High = mean(Value[YearMonth %in% Hi], na.rm = TRUE) / mean(Value, na.rm = TRUE),
              Low  = mean(Value[YearMonth %in% Lo], na.rm = TRUE) / mean(Value, na.rm = TRUE),
              .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(Driver = Alias)

}
```

# Introduction \label{Introduction}

Offshore shocks have dominated recent markets: tariff wars, record global policy uncertainty and sharp swings in oil and gold. This report asks three questions for our investment committee. First, has volatility on the local exchange increased, and does it simply mirror the global experience? Second, how well does our flagship fund, SafeCore, handle that volatility, where does its risk come from, and what factor tilts does it carry? Third, has the opportunity for active managers to add value (alpha) improved since 2020, and how does it move with global conditions?

We follow the standard approach in financial econometrics: measure volatility in several ways (realised, implied and model-based), test whether stress regimes change the behaviour of returns, and judge a portfolio by how it adds up risk, not only by its weights. Section \ref{Data} describes the data and method, Section \ref{Results} reports the results for each question, and Section \ref{Conclusion} concludes with a recommendation.

# Data and Methodology \label{Data}

We use daily total returns for the Capped SWIX (our benchmark), the Top 40, Mid-cap and Small-cap indexes from 2015, and the MSCI All Country World (ACWI) and Emerging Markets (EM) indexes as the global comparison (in USD). Fear gauges include the VIX, V2X and VXEEM implied volatility indexes, the global Economic Policy Uncertainty index (EPU), the MOVE bond volatility index, and USD-ZAR implied volatility (SAVIUSD). SafeCore's monthly holdings are combined with daily stock returns, and Capped SWIX constituent weights (from August 2020) are used for dispersion, correlations and factor exposures.

A few data choices matter. Daily stock returns above +50% or below -50% are treated as data errors and removed. SafeCore's weights only sum to between 79% and 100%, so they are rescaled to 100%. SAVIUSD contains values recorded divided by 100 between 2021 and 2026, which we correct. Finally, the official Low-Volatility index only starts in 2024, so we rebuild it from its constituents back to August 2020; the rebuilt series has a correlation of 0.999 with the official index over their common sample.

**Volatility.** Realised volatility is the annualised standard deviation of daily returns, $\sigma = \sqrt{252}\, sd(r_t)$, measured per calendar year and over a rolling 63-day (three-month) window. To separate signal from noise we fit an AR(1)-GJR-GARCH(1,1) model with a skewed-t distribution [@bollerslev1986; @glosten1993]:

\begin{align}
r_t &= \mu + \phi r_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t = \sqrt{h_t}\, z_t \notag \\
h_t &= \omega + \alpha \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \gamma I_{t-1}\varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta h_{t-1}, \qquad I_{t-1} = 1 \text{ if } \varepsilon_{t-1} < 0 \label{eq1}
\end{align}

Here $\alpha$ is the impact of a new shock, $\gamma$ the extra impact of bad news (the leverage effect) and $\alpha + \beta + \gamma/2$ the persistence of volatility. GJR was chosen over the standard GARCH on information criteria; the more complex eGARCH and apARCH models improved the fit only marginally.

**Stratification.** To link local markets to offshore stress, we flag the months in the top (bottom) 20% of the VIX, global EPU and Brent oil volatility. For each index we compare volatility in those months with its full-sample volatility; a ratio above one means the index is more volatile in that regime.

**Portfolio risk.** SafeCore's daily returns are calculated from its month-end weights, applied from the next trading day. Each stock's share of portfolio risk is its component contribution to portfolio volatility, $w_i (\Sigma w)_i / \sigma_p^2$, using a trailing one-year covariance matrix at each year-end.

**Factor scores.** We build our own Momentum score (the six-month return excluding the latest month) and Low-Volatility score (minus the six-month realised volatility), standardise both across stocks each month, and compare them with the third-party scores. A portfolio's factor exposure is the weighted average score of its holdings.

**Alpha opportunity.** Dispersion is the weighted cross-sectional volatility of Capped SWIX constituents:

\begin{align}
CSV_t = \sqrt{\sum_{i} w_{i,t} \left(R_{i,t} - \bar{R}_t\right)^2}, \qquad \bar{R}_t = \sum_i w_{i,t} R_{i,t} \label{eq2}
\end{align}

We weight by index weight because SafeCore is measured against a cap-weighted benchmark: the alpha it can capture lies where the weight is, and an unweighted measure lets small, illiquid stocks dominate. We pair this with the average pairwise correlation of the 40 largest constituents over a rolling 63-day window, the spread of peer fund returns, and a DCC-GARCH(1,1) model of the correlations between the Financials, Industrials and Resources sectors [@engle2002].

# Results \label{Results}

## Has local volatility increased, and does it mirror the global experience?

Table \ref{tab1} shows that local volatility has no steady upward trend since 2015. It comes in episodes: 2015-16, the COVID crash in 2020, 2022, and again in 2026. Even so, 2026 is the most volatile year outside of COVID for both the Capped SWIX (20.7%) and the Top 40 (22.4%). The local market is also structurally more volatile than the global market, by about two to six percentage points a year.

```{r tab1, results = 'asis'}
Vol_Table(Vol_Rets) %>%
  mutate(across(-Year, ~ round(. * 100, 1))) %>%
  select(Year, `Capped SWIX`, `Top 40`, MidCaps, SmallCaps, ACWI = MSCI_ACWI, EM = MSCI_EM) %>%
  Print_Table(Caption = "Annualised realised volatility (\\%) by calendar year (2026 to September) \\label{tab1}", Digits = 1)
```

```{r Figure1, fig.align = 'center', fig.cap = "Rolling three-month realised volatility: local vs global \\label{Figure1}", fig.height = 3.5, fig.width = 6.5, dev = 'png'}
Roll_Vol_Plot(Vol_Rets %>% filter(Name %in% c("Capped SWIX", "MSCI_ACWI", "MSCI_EM")) %>%
                mutate(Name = recode(Name, MSCI_ACWI = "MSCI ACWI", MSCI_EM = "MSCI EM")), Width = 63)
```

Figure \ref{Figure1} shows that the big spikes are shared with global markets, which points to a common driver. The 2026 spike is the exception: the ACWI stays calm (12.0% for the year), while MSCI EM (25.2%) and the emerging market fear gauge VXEEM (an average of 29.8, against 18.2 for the VIX) surge. The current rise in local volatility is therefore an emerging market risk-off event rather than a global one. With ZAR volatility at its lowest level in the sample, the currency is not the channel either.

```{r garch_fit, include=FALSE}
GARCH_Rets <- Vol_Rets %>% filter(Name %in% c("Capped SWIX", "MSCI_ACWI")) %>%
  mutate(Name = gsub(" ", "_", Name)) %>%
  group_by(Name) %>% arrange(date) %>%
  mutate(dlogret = log(1 + Return)) %>% mutate(scaledret = dlogret - mean(dlogret, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% ungroup()
xts_GARCH <- GARCH_Rets %>% tbl_xts(cols_to_xts = scaledret, spread_by = Name)
Fit_SWIX <- GARCH_Fit(na.omit(xts_GARCH[, "Capped_SWIX"]))
Fit_ACWI <- GARCH_Fit(na.omit(xts_GARCH[, "MSCI_ACWI"]))
Sigmas <- bind_rows(GARCH_Sigma(Fit_SWIX, "Capped SWIX"), GARCH_Sigma(Fit_ACWI, "MSCI ACWI"))
Sigma_Cor <- Sigmas %>% spread(Name, Sigma) %>% na.omit() %>% summarise(cor(`Capped SWIX`, `MSCI ACWI`)) %>% pull()
```

```{r Figure2, fig.align = 'center', fig.cap = "GJR-GARCH(1,1) conditional volatility (annualised) \\label{Figure2}", fig.height = 3.2, fig.width = 6.5, dev = 'png'}
g <- Sigmas %>% ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, Sigma, color = Name), linewidth = 0.7, alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "", y = "Annualised sigma") + fmxdat::theme_fmx()
fmxdat::finplot(g, y.pct = TRUE, y.pct_acc = 1, x.date.type = "%Y", x.date.dist = "1 year")
```

The GARCH results confirm this picture. Ljung-Box tests on squared returns strongly reject the null of no ARCH effects [@engle1982] ($p < 0.001$), which justifies a volatility model. For the Capped SWIX, $\beta = 0.90$ and $\gamma = 0.13$ are highly significant, while $\alpha$ is close to zero: volatility responds to bad news, not good news. Persistence is high (0.965 locally and 0.973 for the ACWI), so shocks fade slowly. The standardised residuals show no remaining ARCH effects. The local and global conditional volatilities in Figure \ref{Figure2} have a correlation of `r round(Sigma_Cor, 2)`.

```{r tab2, results = 'asis'}
Idxs <- Vol_Rets %>% group_by(Name) %>% mutate(Return = Winsor(Return)) %>% ungroup() %>%
  mutate(YearMonth = format(date, "%Y%m"))
bind_rows(
  Perf_comparisons(Idxs, Top_Q(VIX_M), "High VIX"), Perf_comparisons(Idxs, Bot_Q(VIX_M), "Low VIX"),
  Perf_comparisons(Idxs, Top_Q(EPU_M), "High Global EPU"), Perf_comparisons(Idxs, Bot_Q(EPU_M), "Low Global EPU"),
  Perf_comparisons(Idxs, Top_Q(Oil_M), "High Oil Vol"), Perf_comparisons(Idxs, Bot_Q(Oil_M), "Low Oil Vol")) %>%
  select(Name, Period, Ratio) %>% spread(Name, Ratio) %>%
  select(Period, `Capped SWIX`, `Top 40`, MidCaps, SmallCaps, ACWI = MSCI_ACWI, EM = MSCI_EM) %>%
  Print_Table(Caption = "Volatility in each regime relative to full-sample volatility \\label{tab2}")
```

Table \ref{tab2} shows how offshore stress spills over into local markets. In high-VIX months, local volatility runs 30-39% above normal, and in months of high oil volatility it runs 18-30% above normal. In calm months it falls 15-27% below normal. The link with global policy uncertainty is weaker (13-22%), partly because the EPU index has trended upwards, so its high months cluster in 2025 and 2026. These are associations, not proof of causation, but they show clearly that offshore stress changes the risk of holding local equities.

## How does SafeCore navigate volatility?

```{r Figure3, fig.align = 'center', fig.cap = "Rolling three-month volatility: SafeCore, benchmark and Low-Volatility index \\label{Figure3}", fig.height = 3.5, fig.width = 6.5, dev = 'png'}
Roll_Vol_Plot(Compare_Rets %>% mutate(Name = recode(Name, Capped_SWIX = "Capped SWIX", LowVol_Rebuilt = "Low Vol (rebuilt)")), Width = 63)
```

SafeCore does not dampen volatility. Figure \ref{Figure3} shows its volatility sitting on top of the benchmark's throughout, and in 2026 it is slightly higher (21.1% against 20.7%). In high-VIX months its volatility rises by the same amount as the benchmark's (a ratio of 1.31 against 1.33). Table \ref{tab3} shows that since September 2020 its tail risk, measured by Value-at-Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES), and its maximum drawdown (18.5% against 14.1%) are worse than the benchmark's.

```{r tab3, results = 'asis'}
Compare_xts <- Compare_Rets %>% filter(date >= ymd(20200901)) %>%
  tbl_xts(cols_to_xts = Return, spread_by = Name)
Risk_Tab <- rbind(table.AnnualizedReturns(Compare_xts, scale = 252),
                  VaR(Compare_xts, p = 0.95, method = "historical"),
                  ES(Compare_xts, p = 0.95, method = "modified"),
                  maxDrawdown(Compare_xts))
data.frame(Measure = c("Annualised return", "Annualised volatility", "Sharpe ratio (Rf = 0)",
                       "Historical VaR (95%, daily)", "Modified ES (95%, daily)", "Maximum drawdown"),
           Risk_Tab, check.names = FALSE) %>%
  rename(`Capped SWIX` = Capped_SWIX, `Low Vol (rebuilt)` = LowVol_Rebuilt) %>%
  mutate(across(-Measure, ~ round(., 3))) %>%
  Print_Table(Caption = "Risk and return since September 2020 \\label{tab3}", Digits = 3)
```

The fund's strength is returns, not risk control. It has a higher Sharpe ratio, a beta of 0.95, captures 103% of the benchmark's up months and 96% of its down months, and returned more than the benchmark in high-VIX months. In other words, SafeCore has a benchmark-like risk profile with a stock-selection edge. The Low-Volatility index shows what a risk ballast would cost: about 1.5 to 2 percentage points less volatility, but also about 5% less return a year over this period.

```{r risk_contrib, include=FALSE}
Reb_Dates <- SC_Wts %>% distinct(date) %>% filter(format(date, "%m") == "12" | date == max(date)) %>%
  filter(date >= ymd(20151231)) %>% pull(date)
RC <- map_df(Reb_Dates, ~ Risk_Contribution(.x, SC_Wts, Stock_Rets))
RC_Sector <- RC %>% group_by(date, Sector) %>%
  summarise(Weight = sum(Weight), Risk_Share = sum(Risk_Share), .groups = "drop")
```

```{r Figure4, fig.align = 'center', fig.cap = "SafeCore: sector weight vs share of portfolio risk \\label{Figure4}", fig.height = 3.5, fig.width = 6.5, dev = 'png'}
g <- RC_Sector %>% rename(`Share of risk` = Risk_Share) %>%
  gather(Measure, Value, Weight, `Share of risk`) %>%
  ggplot() + geom_col(aes(format(date, "%y"), Value, fill = Sector), position = "stack") +
  facet_wrap(~Measure) + labs(x = "", y = "") + fmxdat::theme_fmx()
fmxdat::finplot(g, y.pct = TRUE)
```

Figure \ref{Figure4} shows where SafeCore's risk comes from. Until 2019 its risk roughly followed its weights, led by Industrials and Financials. By August 2026, Resources hold 40% of the weight but contribute 68% of the risk. Three gold and precious metal miners dominate: AngloGold Ashanti (12% weight, 28% of risk), Gold Fields (7.5%, 17%) and Valterra Platinum (4.4%, 10%). These stocks are both volatile and highly correlated with each other, so together they drive the portfolio. SafeCore has effectively become a single-commodity bet, which leaves it exposed to exactly the offshore and commodity shocks identified above.

```{r factor_prep, include=FALSE}
Own_Scores <- Own_Factor_Scores(Stock_Rets %>% filter(!is.na(Return), date >= ymd(20190101)))
TP_Scores <- Factor_Scores %>% mutate(YM = format(date, "%Y%m")) %>%
  select(YM, Tickers, Factor, Factor_Value) %>% spread(Factor, Factor_Value)
Scores <- inner_join(TP_Scores, Own_Scores, by = c("YM", "Tickers"))
Score_Cors <- Scores %>% group_by(YM) %>%
  summarise(Mom = cor(Own_Momentum, Momentum, method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs"),
            LV = cor(Own_LowVol, `Volatility Sensitivity`, method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs"))
Month_End_Wts <- Local_Index_Constituents %>%
  filter(Index %in% c("Capped SWIX", "LowVol", "Momentum", "Quality", "Value")) %>%
  mutate(YM = format(date, "%Y%m")) %>% group_by(Index, YM) %>% filter(date == max(date)) %>%
  mutate(Weight = weight / sum(weight)) %>% ungroup() %>% select(Portfolio = Index, YM, Tickers, Weight)
All_Wts <- bind_rows(Month_End_Wts, SafeCore %>% mutate(YM = format(date, "%Y%m"), Portfolio = "SafeCore") %>%
                       select(Portfolio, YM, Tickers, Weight))
Exposures <- All_Wts %>% inner_join(Scores, by = c("YM", "Tickers")) %>%
  gather(Factor, Score, -Portfolio, -YM, -Tickers, -Weight) %>%
  group_by(Portfolio, YM, Factor) %>%
  summarise(Exposure = sum(Weight * Score, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(Weight[!is.na(Score)]), .groups = "drop")
```

```{r tab4, results = 'asis'}
Exposures %>% group_by(Portfolio, Factor) %>% summarise(Exposure = mean(Exposure), .groups = "drop") %>%
  spread(Portfolio, Exposure) %>%
  mutate(Factor = recode(Factor, Own_LowVol = "Own Low-Vol", Own_Momentum = "Own Momentum")) %>%
  select(Factor, `Capped SWIX`, SafeCore, LowVol, Momentum, Quality, Value) %>%
  Print_Table(Caption = "Average factor exposure (weighted average z-score), August 2020 to August 2026 \\label{tab4}")
```

Table \ref{tab4} places SafeCore's factor exposures next to the benchmark and four strategy indexes. Relative to the Capped SWIX, SafeCore leans towards Earnings Quality and Value, has a positive and recently growing Momentum tilt (as it rides the gold rally), and has no Low-Volatility tilt. Its Low-Volatility exposure is almost identical to the benchmark's, and has turned slightly negative in 2026.

Our own Momentum score agrees well with the third-party score (an average monthly rank correlation of `r round(mean(Score_Cors$Mom), 2)`), so momentum is a robust signal. Our Low-Volatility score agrees only weakly with the third party's "Volatility Sensitivity" score (`r round(mean(Score_Cors$LV), 2)`). The Low-Volatility index helps us judge which measure to trust: on our realised-volatility score it stands far above the benchmark (0.54 against 0.32), but on the third-party score the two are almost the same. The third-party score therefore appears to measure something else, such as sensitivity to market-wide volatility shocks rather than a stock's own volatility. For a mandate that aims to manage volatility, our realised-volatility score is the more useful one.

## Has the alpha opportunity improved since 2020?

```{r alpha_prep, include=FALSE}
Month_Ends <- SWIX_Cons %>% mutate(YM = format(date, "%Y%m")) %>% group_by(YM) %>%
  filter(date == max(date)) %>% ungroup() %>% distinct(date) %>% filter(date >= ymd(20201130)) %>% pull(date)
Roll_Cor <- map_df(Month_Ends, ~ Avg_Pairwise_Cor(.x, SWIX_Cons, N = 40, LookBack = 63))
Peer_Disp <- Active_Managers %>% filter(date >= ymd(20200901)) %>% group_by(date) %>%
  summarise(Peer_Dispersion = sd(Returns, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
Measures <- bind_rows(
  CSV %>% mutate(YearMonth = format(date, "%Y%m")) %>% group_by(YearMonth) %>%
    summarise(Value = mean(Weighted)) %>% mutate(Measure = "Weighted CSV"),
  Roll_Cor %>% mutate(YearMonth = format(date, "%Y%m"), Measure = "Avg Correlation (Top 40)") %>%
    select(YearMonth, Value = Avg_Cor, Measure),
  Peer_Disp %>% mutate(YearMonth = format(date, "%Y%m"), Measure = "Peer Fund Dispersion") %>%
    select(YearMonth, Value = Peer_Dispersion, Measure))
```

```{r Figure5, fig.align = 'center', fig.cap = "Measures of the alpha opportunity since 2020 (peer fund data end in October 2025) \\label{Figure5}", fig.height = 5.5, fig.width = 6.5, dev = 'png'}
g <- Measures %>% mutate(date = ymd(paste0(YearMonth, "01"))) %>%
  ggplot() + geom_line(aes(date, Value, color = Measure), linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~Measure, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) + labs(x = "", y = "") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx() + theme(legend.position = "none")
fmxdat::finplot(g, x.date.type = "%Y", x.date.dist = "1 year")
```

Figure \ref{Figure5} tracks the alpha opportunity. Dispersion was highest in the recovery after COVID. It then fell steadily to a low in 2024, when the average daily weighted CSV was only 1.63%: correlations were low, but there was little difference between stocks to exploit. Since then dispersion has recovered to 2.03% in 2026, its highest level since 2022, while correlation remains moderate (0.22). This combination of stocks moving apart without moving together makes 2026 the best environment for stock-picking in four years. Weighted and unweighted dispersion are now almost equal, which shows that the spread is coming from the large caps, especially the gold miners pulling away from the rest of the market.

```{r dcc_fit, include=FALSE}
Sector_xts <- SWIX_Cons %>% filter(!is.na(Return)) %>%
  group_by(date, SuperSector) %>% summarise(Return = sum(weight * Return) / sum(weight), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(SuperSector) %>% mutate(dlogret = log(1 + Return), scaledret = dlogret - mean(dlogret)) %>% ungroup() %>%
  tbl_xts(cols_to_xts = scaledret, spread_by = SuperSector)
garch11.spec <- ugarchspec(mean.model = list(armaOrder = c(0, 0)),
                           variance.model = list(garchOrder = c(1, 1), model = "sGARCH"),
                           distribution.model = "norm")
dcc.garch11.spec <- dccspec(uspec = multispec(replicate(3, garch11.spec)), dccOrder = c(1, 1), distribution = "mvnorm")
dcc.fit <- dccfit(dcc.garch11.spec, data = Sector_xts)
Rhot <- rcor(dcc.fit)
DCC_Cors <- tibble(date = as.Date(index(Sector_xts)),
                   `Financials-Industrials` = Rhot[1, 2, ],
                   `Financials-Resources` = Rhot[1, 3, ],
                   `Industrials-Resources` = Rhot[2, 3, ])
```

```{r Figure6, fig.align = 'center', fig.cap = "DCC-GARCH(1,1) conditional correlations between super-sectors \\label{Figure6}", fig.height = 3.2, fig.width = 6.5, dev = 'png'}
g <- DCC_Cors %>% gather(Pair, Rho, -date) %>%
  ggplot() + geom_line(aes(date, Rho, color = Pair), linewidth = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "", y = "Correlation") + fmxdat::theme_fmx()
fmxdat::finplot(g, x.date.type = "%Y", x.date.dist = "1 year")
```

The DCC model in Figure \ref{Figure6} adds a sector view. The multivariate ARCH test rejects the null of no conditional heteroskedasticity ($p < 0.001$), and the DCC parameters are significant ($a = 0.020$, $b = 0.929$), so correlations are time-varying and persistent: a shock to correlations lasts for months, not days. Financials and Industrials move closely together (around 0.55), as both depend on the domestic economy. Resources are the local market's diversifier, with correlations of only 0.2 to 0.3 with the other sectors. This diversification was strongest during the commodity-led decouplings of 2022 and mid-2025, when sector dispersion, and so the alpha opportunity, was highest. It weakens during global stress episodes, when all three correlations rise together.

```{r tab5, results = 'asis'}
Monthly_Driver <- function(df, Nm, FUN = mean) {
  df %>% filter(Name == Nm, date >= ymd(20200901)) %>% mutate(YearMonth = format(date, "%Y%m")) %>%
    group_by(YearMonth) %>% summarise(Level = FUN(TRI))
}
Drivers <- list(
  VIX = Monthly_Driver(Implied_Vol, "VIX"),
  `Global EPU` = Monthly_Driver(Uncertainty_Indexes, "EPUCGLCP", dplyr::last),
  `MOVE (bond vol)` = Monthly_Driver(Uncertainty_Indexes, "MOVE_Index"),
  `ZAR vol` = Local_Cncy_Vol_Index %>% mutate(Name = "SAVIUSD") %>% Monthly_Driver("SAVIUSD"),
  `Oil vol` = Commods %>% filter(Name == "Oil_Brent", date >= ymd(20200801)) %>% arrange(date) %>%
    mutate(Ret = TRI / lag(TRI) - 1, YearMonth = format(date, "%Y%m")) %>% filter(date >= ymd(20200901)) %>%
    group_by(YearMonth) %>% summarise(Level = sd(Ret, na.rm = TRUE) * sqrt(252)))
map2_df(Drivers, names(Drivers), ~ Regime_Means(Measures, .x, .y)) %>%
  gather(Regime, Ratio, High, Low) %>%
  mutate(Col = paste(Measure, Regime, sep = ": ")) %>%
  select(Driver, Col, Ratio) %>% spread(Col, Ratio) %>%
  select(Driver, `Weighted CSV: High`, `Weighted CSV: Low`, `Avg Correlation (Top 40): High`, `Avg Correlation (Top 40): Low`,
         `Peer Fund Dispersion: High`, `Peer Fund Dispersion: Low`) %>%
  setNames(c("Driver", "CSV high", "CSV low", "Corr. high", "Corr. low", "Peer disp. high", "Peer disp. low")) %>%
  Print_Table(Caption = "Alpha-opportunity measures in high and low macro regimes, relative to their average \\label{tab5}")
```

Table \ref{tab5} links the alpha opportunity to global conditions. In high-VIX months dispersion rises by 17%, but stocks also become 23% more correlated. Global stress therefore creates a two-sided opportunity: there is more to gain from picking the right stocks, but more of the market moves together, so the gains go to managers who are positioned correctly on the macro theme. This is why peer fund returns spread out more when the VIX or global policy uncertainty is high (by 18% and 20%). Oil volatility raises both dispersion and correlation, as commodity shocks split the market into Resources and the rest. Bond market volatility (MOVE) raises correlation without raising dispersion, which is the least helpful combination for stock-pickers. The sample is short (73 months), so these regime effects should be read as indicative.

# Conclusion \label{Conclusion}

Local volatility has not risen steadily, but it is high again in 2026, and it is driven mainly from offshore. It shares its major spikes with global markets, but the 2026 episode tracks emerging markets, and periods of high global stress raise local volatility by about a third. SafeCore has delivered alpha, but it does nothing to dampen this volatility, and its risk is now concentrated in a handful of gold miners. The opportunity to add value through stock selection has improved to its best level since 2022, yet the macro regimes that create this opportunity are the same ones that make stocks fall together.

We therefore recommend keeping SafeCore's stock-selection process, but adding a deliberate risk ballast: a cap on the share of risk any one sector can contribute, a tilt towards low-volatility stocks using our realised-volatility score, and regular monitoring of offshore stress indicators such as the VIX, VXEEM and oil volatility. This would let the fund keep its edge while limiting the damage when global storms reach local shores.
